images.title: Copies of one sharing
images.purpose: Show that 4 rotis for 6 children and 6 rotis for 9 children are 2 and 3 copies of 2 rotis for 3 children, so the share stays 2/3.
images.composition: Three rows stacked with wide gaps: 1 tile, then 2 tiles, then 3 tiles, left edges lined up, each row with its fraction at the right end.
images.exact_structure: Each tile is the same rounded rectangle, outlined teal #0072B2, holding 2 small round rotis of the same size and no text. Row 1: 1 tile, with the one caption just above it. Row 2: 2 identical tiles side by side. Row 3: 3 identical tiles side by side. Tiles in all rows are exactly the same size and spacing. A fraction sits at the right end of each row in amber #E69F00. Result line centred at the bottom. No children drawn. Exactly 6 tiles and 12 rotis.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
tiles of different sizes, or the caption 2 rotis, 3 children written more than once
images.takeaway: Copies of the same sharing give the same share, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9.
images.description: Three rows of identical tiles, 1, 2 and 3 tiles, each tile holding 2 rotis for 3 children; the rows are labelled 2/3, 4/6 and 6/9, all the same share.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to count the tiles in each row and say why more copies of the same tile do not change each child's share.

image_decisions.why: Seeing bigger groups as copies of the smallest group is a picture idea; one image of tile rows carries it.
